projects.summary: An AI-assisted studio for branching visual novels. Write with an assistant, generate reviewed art and voices, and ship a Godot game.
projects.readme:
# FlintGraph

FlintGraph is an AI-assisted visual-novel Studio. Write scenes, build branching
choices, stage characters and illustrations, playtest in the browser, and export
an editable Godot/GDScript game.

The creator owns the story. The Assistant proposes changes for review; accepting
a proposal creates a revision. Gameplay follows the authored story and needs no
AI service or FlintGraph account.

![A visual-novel playtest with an illustrated train-carriage scene and dialogue](docs/reports/evidence/scene-art-cgs-2026-10-31/04-playtest.png)

*Play a saved story in the browser, with dialogue over a full-screen event CG.*

The local Studio, Godot player, browser playtests and release downloads are
implemented. The project is under active development; the
[roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md#narrative-game-studio) separates
completed work from the next milestones.

## Make a visual novel

| In the Studio | What you can do |
| --- | --- |
| Assistant | Describe a scene or character, inspect streamed progress, review proposed edits, and accept them into the story. Image suggestions become jobs when you choose Generate. |
| Write and Map | Edit scene scripts, dialogue, choices and state; organize scenes in folders; inspect branching routes. |
| Characters and Assets | Upload art, approve generated candidates, manage backgrounds, sprites, expressions and CGs, and organize the library. |
| Stage and Look | Place and frame characters, change backgrounds and expressions, show full-screen event CGs under the dialogue, and edit the game's theme. |
| Voices | Upload line audio or generate it with a configured local model; choose character voices and per-line delivery. Cloned voices require consented references and applicable license acceptance. |
| Reviewed looks | Lock an approved reference with edited hair, eye and clothing tags; reuse named looks for new requests and save side-by-side character/clothes feedback. Optional clothing-tag comparisons stay advisory. |
| Poses and training | Generate poses from an approved look, choose seated, standing or walking body guides, repair a selected area, and train private character/style versions from reviewed images. |
| Playtest and Releases | Test the saved story in the isolated Godot preview, then build and download a web game or editable Godot source. |

The player supports authored choices and conditions, local saves, voice volume,
and a CG gallery that unlocks illustrations as they are seen. CGs cover the stage
while dialogue continues; clearing them reveals the background and characters
underneath.

![The scene editor with a scene hierarchy, event CG, character placement and dialogue](docs/reports/evidence/scene-art-cgs-2026-10-31/03-stage-event-cg.png)

*Arrange scenes, set the stage and edit the dialogue in one writing desk.*

Projects keep immutable revisions and recoverable edit conflicts. Uploaded and
generated assets record provenance, hashes, approval and rights declarations.
Releases capture a particular story and its approved assets with versioned build
metadata and notices. Private model weights and Studio look metadata stay out of
the game.

## Run the narrative Studio

You need Python 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+,
and configured PostgreSQL, MinIO and Temporal services. Docker is used for local
fixtures and isolated release builds. Browser playtests need the verified Godot
engine/templates and a prepared preview build. AI workers additionally need their
separate model installations; authoring with uploaded assets does not require
image or voice generation.

From the repository root, in PowerShell:

```powershell
uv sync --all-groups
npm --prefix frontend ci
Copy-Item tools/narrative/studio.env.example studio.local.env
```

Fill in the new `studio.local.env` using the
[Studio runbook](docs/runbooks/narrative-studio.md#start-everything). It is private
and git-ignored; use your own service settings, model pins, prepared preview and
builder paths. The example is a configuration template, not a ready-made model
installation. Skip the copy step if you already have a local configuration.

Once dependencies and configuration are prepared:

```powershell
uv run python tools/narrative/studio.py check
uv run python tools/narrative/studio.py
```

Open **http://localhost:5173**. The launcher starts the configured containers,
waits for dependencies, applies migrations, and runs the selected API, workers,
relay, preview and frontend. It refuses occupied ports or a stale preview build.
Ctrl+C stops the processes it started. `check` can start configured containers to
check dependencies, but does not launch the Studio processes or apply migrations.

`STUDIO_SERVICES` chooses which processes run. For manual authoring without model
workers, configure the subset described in the runbook. Ollama powers the local
Assistant; image and voice inference run in isolated worker environments.
Downloads, GPU requirements and model/license pins are explicit setup steps.

For a smaller introduction without the Studio services, follow
[play the original sample locally](docs/runbooks/narrative-local-play.md), then
[export and play it in Godot or the browser](docs/runbooks/narrative-web-play.md).

## Models and character consistency

Local image tools include Animagine XL character/background generation, optional
transparent sprite cutouts, face-only expression repainting and reference-guided
CG generation. Poses use a separately installed FLUX.2 klein 4B editing model.
Voice choices and their installation/license requirements are documented in the
[voice runbook](docs/runbooks/narrative-voice-generation.md). Nothing downloads
model weights merely by opening an exported game.

Reviewed looks freeze the words used for new portraits and the approved reference
used for expressions and CGs. A deliberate outfit change gets a new named look.
You still review every candidate: image references do not guarantee identity or
clothing fidelity, especially in two-character CGs. Clothing-tag overlap misses
fine details and does not determine approval.

![The pose workbench showing an approved character reference, walking skeleton and editable pose description](docs/reports/standing-walking-guides-2026-11-02/studio-walking-desktop.png)

*Use the approved look for appearance and a body guide for pose geometry.*

The pose workbench supports an additional approved appearance view or a body
guide, local area repairs, and private character/style LoRA versions trained from
explicitly selected, approved images. Character and style versions can be combined
within a bounded strength budget. Training is a local worker job; optional MLflow
tracking records numeric metrics and hashes. Training images and weights stay out
of exported games.

Optional per-image tag suggestions help prepare content captions. Review and edit
each proposal before applying it; manual entry remains available.

Check anatomy, costume details, linework and lighting before approval. Known
anatomically flawed images are excluded from training, but guides and trained
versions do not guarantee a correct result. Automatic calibrated CCIP identity
scoring, per-character CG scoring and candidate ranking remain unfinished.

See the [body-guide examples and limits](docs/reports/2026-11-02-standing-and-walking-guides.md),
[character/style training](docs/reports/2026-11-02-combined-pose-adapters.md) and
[measurement research](docs/reports/2026-11-01-character-preservation.md).
The screenshots above use qualification fixtures documented in the delivery reports.

## Documentation

- [Studio workflow and local setup](docs/runbooks/narrative-studio.md)
- [Assistant and reviewed proposals](docs/runbooks/narrative-assistant.md)
- [Image generation, expressions, CGs and reviewed looks](docs/runbooks/narrative-image-generation.md)
- [Voice generation and model licenses](docs/runbooks/narrative-voice-generation.md)
- [Godot toolchain](docs/runbooks/godot-toolchain.md) and [player contract](docs/architecture/godot-player-contract.md)
- [Product direction](docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md), [delivery queue](docs/product/narrative-game-backlog.md) and [roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md)
- [Reviewed prompt catalog and Langfuse setup](docs/runbooks/prompt-management.md)
- [Workspace security](docs/architecture/security-boundary.md) and [deployment hardening](docs/runbooks/deployment-hardening.md)

## Development checks

```powershell
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check .
uv run mypy
$env:FLINT_GRAPH_ENV = "test"
uv run alembic upgrade head --sql
docker compose config
npm --prefix frontend test
npm --prefix frontend run typecheck
npm --prefix frontend run build
```

Default tests use deterministic offline model behavior. Real PostgreSQL, Godot,
browser, worker and model qualification have additional fixtures and opt-in
settings documented in the relevant runbooks and delivery reports. Shared
retrieval services have an additional evaluation gate:

```powershell
uv run flint-graph-eval run --dataset evals/datasets/acme-smoke --evaluations evals/reports/acme-smoke/deterministic-recorded.jsonl --experiment evals/experiments/acme-smoke.yaml --baseline evals/reports/acme-smoke/baselines.json --config-name deterministic
```

## Shared platform services

FlintGraph includes ingestion, extraction, knowledge graph, retrieval and
grounded-answer APIs for document and context workflows.
PostgreSQL is the system of record; MinIO stores immutable artifacts; Temporal
handles durable jobs. Workspace authorization, revision and job boundaries,
storage and observability support the Studio and its shared services.

`docker compose up --build` starts the shared-service stack; the Studio uses
the launcher above. For document workflows, use the
[developer profiles](docs/runbooks/developer-profiles.md),
[local Ollama RAG guide](docs/runbooks/local-ollama-rag.md), and
[service milestone documentation](docs/milestones/). Operational guidance
covers [observability, audit and usage](docs/runbooks/operations-observability.md)
and [backup/restore](docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md).

`X-Tenant-ID` selects a workspace; OIDC authentication and server-side membership
authorize access. Production deployment still requires explicit secrets,
exposure settings, private backing services and operational qualification. See
the security and deployment guides before exposing the API.

milestones.description: Planning only: PostgreSQL-authoritative, tenant-scoped user-visible research artifacts on existing object storage, capability-gated isolated tool execution, budgets, provenance, retention and security qualification. Coordinate M18/M20/M22; no default arbitrary-code execution.

milestones.title: Milestone 29: agent security and safety qualification
milestones.description: In progress: threat-model/ADR 0029 design baseline and synthetic required-case catalog delivered (#80); URL user-info rejection (#103) and connection-bound DNS/redirect/TLS/deadline controls (#104, ADR 0030) qualified with red-first tests, isolated real sockets, deployed API and green CI. Runtime controls #81, deployment egress, capability/approval, memory/cache, sandbox and budget qualification remain open. This is not security certification; coordinate M18/M20/M22/M28/M25.

milestones.title: Milestone 30: portable story runtime and Godot proof
milestones.description:
A versioned portable narrative package, deterministic execution/save semantics, trusted Godot source export and actual engine/browser conformance. Written M30 spec review precedes implementation.

Product direction: https://github.com/mohripan/flint-graph/blob/master/docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md

milestones.title: Milestone 31: authored narrative game studio
milestones.description:
Project/revision authorization, a manual scene-and-choice editor, shared-runtime browser preview and immutable release downloads. Depends on M30; no AI required for manual creation.

Product direction: https://github.com/mohripan/flint-graph/blob/master/docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md

milestones.title: Milestone 32: reviewed narrative assistance and continuity
milestones.description:
Project-scoped source/canon and character knowledge, bounded proposal jobs, explicit diff acceptance and dependency-aware continuity revisions. Depends on M31; focused subsystem designs required.

Product direction: https://github.com/mohripan/flint-graph/blob/master/docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md

milestones.title: Milestone 33: controlled game asset production
milestones.description:
Project-scoped art library, reviewed references, bounded image jobs, asset approval/provenance and release bindings. Depends on M31; uploaded art works without an image model.

Product direction: https://github.com/mohripan/flint-graph/blob/master/docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md

milestones.title: Milestone 34: narrative game release qualification
milestones.description:
An original complete game with three reachable endings, measured 15–30 minute human playtest, live browser/Godot proof, nightly route gates and recovery/security/performance evidence. Depends on M31–33.

Product direction: https://github.com/mohripan/flint-graph/blob/master/docs/product/narrative-game-studio.md

milestones.title: Milestone 35: versioned prompt management with Langfuse
milestones.description: Prompts become managed, versioned, evaluated artifacts: authored and promoted with labels in self-hosted Langfuse, a committed prompt lock for offline and outage reproducibility, eval-gated promotion and exact prompt identity on every model call. Runtime never blocks on Langfuse. Coordinates #79 and M32. Tracking issue #133.

milestones.title: Milestone 36: context engineering and token budgets
milestones.description: Every model call assembles context from an explicit, measured budget: provider-accurate token counts, reserved slices for instructions, history, memory, evidence, tools and output, provider prompt caching for stable prefixes, and an inspectable per-call context manifest. Serves M27 and M32; coordinates #82, #83 and #63. Tracking issue #141.

milestones.title: Milestone 37: durable memory with user controls
milestones.description: Governed memory beyond the current turn: the conversation memory policy selected in #75, opt-in user/workspace/project memory with review and erase controls, narrative context from accepted canon with per-character knowledge views, and poisoning/leakage qualification. PostgreSQL-authoritative; remembered content is never evidence. Tracking issue #151.

milestones.title: Milestone 38: visual novel characters, backgrounds and staging
milestones.description: Visual novel presentation beyond v1's single portrait and background: layered 2D character sprites with expressions and outfits built in a studio character creator, multi-character staging, backgrounds with variants and a CG gallery, transitions, audio, a themed player UI and standard VN controls. Deterministic, save-safe and identical across browser preview and Godot export. Depends on M31 and #128. Tracking issue #156.

milestones.title: Milestone 39: expressive and cloned character voices
milestones.description: Characters speak in a creator's own or a consenting speaker's voice from a short reference, and lines can be delivered angry, sad, whispered or dramatic. Local and offline; generated clips stay reviewed candidates; reference audio never ships. Builds on ADR 0043 (line voices, Kokoro worker). Tracking issue #173.

milestones.title: Milestone 40: consistent characters across poses, outfits and scenes
milestones.description: A character generated once keeps the same face, hair and clothes in later poses, expressions and CGs. Research CCIP identity and outfit scores (deepghs ccip/imgutils), locked looks, local LoRA fine-tuning, richer references and context, and pose methods on a shared bench, then build the winners in. Local and offline. Tracking issue #179.

milestones.title: Milestone 41: coordinated GPU resources and multi-node production path
milestones.description: Coordinate image, audio and local LLM admission on native Windows using NVML, a custom host-local GPU broker and existing Temporal/Ollama. Measure dedicated VRAM, preserve external ownership, qualify fenced leases/fairness/recovery, and expose useful queue state. Production is Linux on multiple IaaS nodes with Kubernetes; cloud vs on-premises remains undecided. Define the node-placement/routing/admission contract without making Kubernetes a local prerequisite. Ray and Linux MPS/MIG remain optional evidence-based follow-ups, not defaults. Planning only; live hardware/cluster qualification and rollout gates are explicit. Tracking issue #187.

milestones.title: Milestone 42: AWS deployment with a GPU that sleeps when idle
milestones.description: First cloud stage: an always-on CPU tier and one GPU instance that starts when generation is queued and stops itself after an idle period, so GPU time is paid only while generating. Precedes the multi-node Kubernetes path in M41 (#194). Tracking issue #195.

projects.name: Capsulet
projects.summary: Correctness-first AI-agent workflows. Typed graphs on a durable worker, governed memory, and a deterministic kernel that issues certificates.
projects.readme:
<!-- capsulet-claims: CAP-PRODUCT-001, CAP-CORRECTNESS-001, CAP-CORRECTNESS-002, CAP-GRAPH-001, CAP-AGENT-001, CAP-AGENT-002, CAP-AGENT-003, CAP-AGENT-004, CAP-AGENT-005, CAP-AGENT-006, CAP-AGENT-007, CAP-MEMORY-001, CAP-JOB-001, CAP-WORKFLOW-001, CAP-AUTOMATION-001, CAP-IAM-001, CAP-PERSISTENCE-001, CAP-DASHBOARD-001, CAP-SDK-001, CAP-OBSERVABILITY-001, CAP-SECURITY-001, CAP-HELM-001, CAP-CORRECTNESS-013 -->
# Capsulet

Capsulet is a correctness-first AI-agent workflow platform for building and operating workflows
whose important outputs can be inspected, checked, and governed.

The product has three layers: an implemented workflow/job engine for deterministic execution and
compatibility, an experimental agent platform with typed graphs, a durable worker that executes them, and
governed memory, and a correctness plane whose deterministic kernel is implemented but whose runtime-wide admission and
assurance model is planned. See the
[product constitution](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-correctness-first-agent-workflow-platform-design.md)
and the [public claim registry](docs/contracts/product-claims.md) for the authoritative boundaries.
Public stability, migration, lifecycle, and SDK rules are indexed in
[docs/contracts](docs/contracts/README.md).

For a deterministic local check that needs no service containers, run
`cargo run -p capsulet-xtask --locked -- verify --profile fast`. The full release-equivalent graph
is `verify --profile full`; inspect its machine-readable definition with
`verify --list --format json`.

![Capsulet workflow dashboard](docs/images/capsulet-dashboard.png)

## What works today

- typed agent graph definitions with nodes, ports, hyperedges, transition policies, and static execution order
- agent definitions with graph references, step/token/time/cost budgets, and termination policies
- agent runs executed by a dedicated durable worker, with deterministic nodes, local-model nodes, memory reads, validators, and job and memory-write effects that happen once per run
- validators that send an agent round again until it passes or a budget stops it, with usage and every step readable from the run's log
- cancelling a run, and approving or refusing one waiting at a human gate, over the API
- claim-first memory records for sources, evidence, entities, claims, events, relationships, and contract DSL summaries
- nested memory subgraphs with owner, schema, permissions, summary-claim, summary-trace, membership, activation, canonical entity, graph attachment, and explicit cross-subgraph edge primitives
- deterministic local ingestion that proposes candidate claims and evidence-backed memory from uploaded text
- human review queues for candidate claims, entity-resolution proposals, and conflicting active claims
- reusable Python job definitions with JSON input schemas and retry policies
- compatibility workflow DAGs with parallel roots, fan-out, and fan-in dependencies
- manual, timezone-aware cron, read-only SQL, signed webhook, and isolated custom-plugin triggers
- bearer authentication with viewer/operator/admin authorization and durable mutation auditing
- durable PostgreSQL agent, graph, job, attempt, workflow-step, log, and artifact metadata
- stub, trusted local process, WASI Python, and Kubernetes Job runners
- S3-compatible or filesystem artifact storage
- enforced execution-pool concurrency, cancellation, timeouts, delayed retry, and stale-lease recovery
- owner-bound worker heartbeats and finalization that fence stale workers after lease adoption
- workflow resume from successful step checkpoints after failure or timeout
- Kubernetes Job reattachment after worker failure
- API, worker, scheduler, and evaluator health and Prometheus metrics endpoints
- configurable artifact, log, trigger-event, and audit retention cleanup
- Docker Compose for local use and a Helm chart for Kubernetes

## Product layers

Capsulet is organized as three cooperating layers:

- **Workflow engine (implemented compatibility infrastructure):** durable jobs, runners, workflow
  DAGs, triggers, retries, cancellation, logs, and artifacts.
- **Agent platform (experimental):** typed agent definitions and static execution graphs, budgets,
  validators that drive a bounded loop, and a durable worker that executes them against governed
  memory and a local model. A graph where a model chooses the next node cannot run yet and is refused
  at run start, and a finished run is `unverified`: nothing has checked its result.
- **Correctness plane (implemented kernel slice; planned platform enforcement):** proposals,
  deterministic checks, evidence, residual obligations, and certificates. Runtime-wide protected
  boundary admission and the unified verified-computation IR are not implemented yet.

Governed memory is a major agent-platform subsystem, not Capsulet's complete identity. It models
claims, entities, events, relationships, evidence, permissions, source authority, contradictions,
review state, and nested contexts.

An agent definition binds a graph to a control envelope: iterations, tokens, runtime seconds, cost, and explicit termination conditions. Starting a run compiles the agent into a versioned definition, and the graph worker executes it as a bounded loop. Node configuration is part of that version, so changing a prompt makes a new one. A failed validator sends the run round again with what its last attempt left. A budget, a lack of progress, a safety check or a person's refusal ends it as `stopped`, never as `succeeded`.

```text
state -> agent-enter -> (your graph) -> agent-continue -> agent-leave -> state
                             |                 |
                             v                 v
                   event log and usage    go round again?
```

The memory graph is claim-first. A claim records what was said, who or what it is about, where it came from, when it was observed or valid, its confidence, and its review state. Nested subgraphs provide bounded memory contexts for teams, projects, customers, incidents, or personal modules. Each active subgraph must have an owner, schema, permissions, summary claim, and traceability from that summary back to inner claims or evidence. Canonical entities connect local entities across subgraphs without erasing context-specific disagreement.

```text
raw text -> source/evidence -> candidate claims -> review -> active memory
                                           |             |
                                           v             v
                                  entity resolution   conflict inbox
```

## Correctness direction and current boundary

The deterministic three-valued kernel and a narrow reasoning/certificate API slice are implemented.
The four-valued platform assurance model, trust-typed workflow IR, universal admission checks, and
durable looping graph worker are planned. The full direction is in the
[product constitution](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-correctness-first-agent-workflow-platform-design.md);
the narrower proposer/checker foundation remains in
[docs/design/correctness-architecture.md](docs/design/correctness-architecture.md) and
[ADR 0012](docs/adr/0012-correctness-kernel-and-proposer-checker-split.md).

The goal is not to replace frontier models. It is to make a small model good enough for complex
work, by making correctness a property of the system rather than of the model. Small models are
poor at long chains and roughly adequate at single hops, so the plan is to only ever ask for a
single hop and move composition into deterministic mechanisms that can check it explicitly.

That requires being precise about what can be checked. Whether an id exists, whether a claim is
active, whether a quoted string is byte-identical to the span it cites, whether arithmetic
recomputes, whether two intervals overlap, whether a predicate is declared with that arity —
all of these are mechanically decidable with no model in the loop. Whether a passage *means* what
a claim says it means is not, and no amount of architecture changes that.

So the boundary becomes the product. A node returns a proposal rather than a value; a
deterministic kernel with no learned component decides it and emits a certificate; and the
verdict is three-valued. **Accepted** means every step was discharged mechanically. **Conditional**
means the result is sound given a set of named readings, each pinned to a span. **Rejected** names
the failed premise and the subsystem that owns the repair. For contract-declared number, money,
and date objects, citations compare exact values rather than their spelling. An unresolved shared
currency symbol or numeric day/month date is an evidence-linked residual, never a guessed value
(`CAP-CORRECTNESS-013`). Capsulet does not verify meaning today
either — the difference is that it would stop implying otherwise, and report per answer exactly
what was mechanically discharged and what was assumed.

Learned components stay on the proposer side of that line. Knowledge graph embeddings are
well suited to generating retrieval candidates and ordering search, and unsuited to deciding
truth; an embedding score never appears in a certificate.

```text
proposer -> kernel (deterministic) -> certificate
            no model, no network       verdict + discharged steps
            no I/O beyond the store    + residual obligations
```

## How execution stays durable

PostgreSQL is the source of truth. An agent run's status is a fold over its append-only event log, so a worker that dies mid-run loses nothing: the next one reads the log and carries on. Effects are claimed before they are attempted, so a job or a memory write happens once however many workers it takes. See [ADR 0019](docs/adr/0019-agent-runs-execute-on-the-durable-path.md).

The existing job runner path remains durable as the lower-level execution substrate. A worker atomically leases a queued job, records the attempt, and renews the lease while execution is active. After lease expiry, non-reattachable work is requeued; Kubernetes work can be adopted by another worker without incrementing the attempt count. Heartbeat and finalization both require the current lease owner, so the previous worker cannot commit a result after adoption. See [ADR 0013](docs/adr/0013-owner-bound-finalization-for-adoptable-job-attempts.md).

Compatibility workflow nodes still have durable step runs. Successful nodes are checkpoints: their metadata and artifacts remain complete even when another branch fails. Calling the resume endpoint removes only unsuccessful attempts and lets the scheduler reconstruct the missing runnable nodes from the saved graph state.

## Local Docker Compose

Prerequisites: Docker with Compose v2.

```sh
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps
```

Open the dashboard at <http://127.0.0.1:3000> and the API at <http://127.0.0.1:8080>.

The local stack includes PostgreSQL, Mailpit, API, worker, graph worker, scheduler, evaluator, and dashboard. Objects are stored on a shared volume, because MinIO no longer publishes the community images the stack used. Compose waits on dependency health and restarts long-running services after failure. Sign in with the development token `capsulet-local-admin-token-change-me`; replace it before exposing the stack.

Useful checks:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/livez
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics
docker compose logs -f api worker graph-worker scheduler evaluator
```

Stop the stack without deleting persisted volumes:

```sh
docker compose down
```

## Agent execution graph API

Create typed graphs, bind them to agents, and start agent runs:

```sh
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/graphs
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agents
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agents/<agent-id>/runs
```

Read a run, read its log, and act on it:

```sh
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agent-runs/<run-id>
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agent-runs/<run-id>/events
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agent-runs/<run-id>/cancel
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"approved":true}' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/agent-runs/<run-id>/decisions
```

Model nodes use a local [Ollama](https://ollama.com) at `CAPSULET_OLLAMA_URL`. With none reachable they
fail and say so, and everything deterministic still runs. See [the API guide](docs/api.md#agents-and-agent-runs)
for what a node can be configured to do. `scripts/agent-smoke.ps1` runs agents through the stack, killing
the worker mid-run.

## Memory Studio API

Memory APIs are tenant/project scoped and claim-first. They support direct authoring, deterministic ingestion, review, and nested graph governance:

```sh
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/memory/sources
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/memory/claims
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/ingestion/review/claims?status=candidate
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/memory/entity-resolutions?status=candidate
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/memory/conflicts?status=candidate
```

The dashboard Memory Studio exposes ingestion, claim review, entity resolution, nested graph activation, and the conflict inbox as the first product surface for governing memory before agents consume it.

## Kernel certificate API

The first slice of the correctness architecture is implemented: stored text is
cut into byte-exact citable spans, retrieval pins the legal evidence set, a local
model proposes a derivation, and a deterministic kernel decides it. The response
is a certificate, not a bare answer.

Requires a local [Ollama](https://ollama.com) with a small model pulled. The
proposer runs outside the stack on purpose — correctness does not depend on it:

```sh
ollama pull qwen2.5:1.5b
# Ollama must accept traffic from the containers
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 ollama serve
```

```sh
curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"text":"Acme renewed the Contoso contract on 2026-03-01. Notice is 30 days.",
       "question":"When was the contract renewed?",
       "contract_id":"<a memory contract whose relations declare stated_by phrasings>"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/reasoning/ask

curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/reasoning/certificates
```

Verdicts are three-valued. **accepted** means every step was discharged
mechanically: the cited span re-derived byte-for-byte from the stored source and
states the claim in a phrasing its memory contract declares for the relation, in
one sentence that does not deny, hedge or question it. **conditional** means the
derivation required a reading, which is recorded as a residual obligation pinned
to the span it came from — which is every answer when no `contract_id` is given,
because then no relation has a declared phrasing to be stated in. **rejected** names the failed premise and the subsystem that
owns the repair, so a dangling reference re-runs retrieval instead of re-prompting
the model.

Persisted kernel proposals always identify their schema. Offline replay reads a
versionless legacy proposal as v1, refuses unsupported proposal versions as unreadable,
and keeps malformed v1 input distinct; it does not claim a verdict for unreadable input.

Two limits are deliberate and documented: a declared phrasing is matched, not
entailed — a sentence can still doubt it in words no cue list knows — and
relevance to the question is not checked at all. See
[the design note](docs/design/correctness-architecture.md).

## Compatibility workflow recovery API

Resume a failed or timed-out workflow run:

```sh
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/workflow-runs/<run-id>/resume
```

The response contains the workflow run and preserved successful step runs. Active, queued, cancelled, removed, and successful runs are rejected to avoid ambiguous recovery.

## Kubernetes with Helm

The chart installs the API, worker, graph worker, scheduler, evaluator, dashboard, migration job, separated control-plane/execution service accounts, default-deny execution network policy, services, configuration, and optional bundled PostgreSQL and MinIO.

```sh
helm lint charts/capsulet
kubectl create namespace capsulet
kubectl create secret generic capsulet-api-auth \
  --namespace capsulet \
  --from-literal='tokens=[{"name":"cluster-admin","role":"admin","token":"replace-with-at-least-32-random-characters"}]'
helm install capsulet charts/capsulet \
  --namespace capsulet \
  --set api.auth.existingSecret=capsulet-api-auth

kubectl wait --for=condition=available deployment \
  --all --namespace capsulet --timeout=5m
kubectl port-forward service/capsulet-dashboard 3000:80 --namespace capsulet
```

Production deployments should use external managed PostgreSQL and object storage, immutable image tags, network policies, and dedicated execution capacity. Capsulet constrains execution pods but does not claim to be a complete sandbox for hostile code.

See [installation](docs/installation.md), [Helm values](docs/helm-values.md), and [worker/runner design](docs/worker-runner.md) for configuration details.

## Repository layout

```text
crates/
  application/  application services, agent runtime use cases, and ports
  api/          HTTP control plane
  core/         domain types, state machines, and validation rules
  postgres/     SQLx persistence and migrations
  runner/       runner contracts plus stub, process, WASI, and Kubernetes adapters
  scheduler/    compatibility automation triggering and DAG reconciliation
  evaluator/    durable trigger evaluation and retention cleanup
  worker/       lower-level job runtime loop, runner selection, and health endpoints
  graph-worker/ durable worker that executes agent runs and IR runs
  storage/      filesystem and S3-compatible object storage
  cli/          command-line client
dashboard/      Next.js dashboard
sdk/python/     decorator-based Python workflow SDK
charts/capsulet Helm chart
migrations/     PostgreSQL schema history
```

## Development and verification

The repository's product vocabulary and public contract inventory have one local/CI gate:

```powershell
pwsh ./scripts/check-contracts.ps1
```

It checks claim evidence and generated claim docs, lifecycle/assurance mappings, accepted ADR
evidence, generated OpenAPI/runtime parity, authorization metadata, deterministic artifacts, and
the experimental Python/dashboard operation maps. See the [public contracts](docs/contracts/README.md)
and [development guide](docs/development.md) before changing a public claim, endpoint, status, or
client call.

### Python workflow authoring

Python workflows are still available as a compatibility authoring path and as a useful substrate for deterministic agent tools. They can be authored as decorated Python functions or as Python cells in the dashboard notebook. The [CSV artifact pipeline](examples/workflows/csv_pipeline.py) creates a CSV in one task, passes it to a dependent task, and downloads the transformed artifact. See the [example instructions](examples/workflows/README.md) for the end-to-end commands.

Rust is pinned to version 1.96.0. The dashboard requires Node.js 20 or newer.

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --locked

cd dashboard
npm ci
npm test
npm run build
npm run test:e2e
```

Database integration tests require `CAPSULET_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, naming a server on which each test binary creates a database of its own. Full local and Kubernetes validation steps are documented in [development](docs/development.md).

## Documentation

- [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md)
- [Correctness architecture (direction)](docs/design/correctness-architecture.md)
- [API](docs/api.md)
- [Development](docs/development.md)
- [Installation](docs/installation.md)
- [Persistence](docs/persistence.md)

projects.name: Capsulet Mesh Train
projects.summary: Custom transports and collective algorithms for distributed training, built in C++ with planned PyTorch integration.
projects.readme:
# capsulet-mesh-train

A distributed training communication engine built in C++, with PyTorch integration.

The core project implements its own transport and collective algorithms. GPU training is the main target; a four-process CPU trainer establishes correctness first. Existing communication libraries and training frameworks can attach through adapters.

## Current state

M1 and M2 are complete for Linux CPU local/container operation and shared-single-GPU functional training. The standalone C++ core implements blocking centralized FP32 SUM all-reduce over its own Linux TCP transport, with bounded failures and safe cleanup. Native validation covers 1–5 worker processes, exact/random numerical checks, failure scenarios, and four independent containers. The optional Python package exposes strict in-place NumPy buffers with retained ownership and GIL release. The optional PyTorch MLP trainer passes four-worker/100-step parity against an independent combined-batch reference, with explicit gradient averaging and rank diagnostics. The same 100-step workload passes in four independent Linux containers. Clean builds, controlled native failure groups and scoped cleanup pass locally and in [full CI](https://github.com/mohripan/capsulet-mesh-train/actions/runs/39030243246). The optional [host-staged CUDA adapter](docs/CUDA.md) also passes installed one/two-worker functional checks on the laptop GPU. The optional [CUDA MLP trainer](docs/CUDA_TRAINING.md) passes two-worker/100-step independent GPU reference parity in pinned and pageable modes. Both workers share the laptop GPU; [GPU/CI evidence](docs/openspecs/cuda-mlp-trainer/verification.md) records actual results and remaining limits. M3/#13 adds [explicit native ring SUM](docs/RING.md), duplex TCP and wire v2, with local conformance/package/container checks and [exact-revision CI](https://github.com/mohripan/capsulet-mesh-train/actions/runs/39127401157) passed. #13 is closed; next is #14's tree reduction OpenSpec. Python and trainers retain their centralized defaults.

This is an open-ended side project. Milestones describe outcomes and dependencies, with no dates or time estimates.

## Start here

- [Roadmap and milestone completion criteria](docs/ROADMAP.md)
- [Build instructions and verified environments](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md)
- [Native ring selection, protocol upgrade and focused checks](docs/RING.md)
- [Python package, API and focused verification](docs/PYTHON.md)
- [Host-staged CUDA tensor SUM and hardware evidence](docs/CUDA.md)
- [CUDA model training and independent GPU reference](docs/CUDA_TRAINING.md)
- [Run the CPU trainer and inspect numerical evidence](docs/TRAINING.md)
- [Reproduce native failures and four-container M1 validation](docs/VALIDATION.md)
- [CPU MVP design](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-16-cpu-mvp-design.md)
- [Decisions and their rationale](docs/DECISIONS.md)
- [Architecture decision records](docs/adr/README.md)
- [GitHub work index](docs/ISSUES.md)
- [Contributor and agent navigation](AGENTS.md)
- [Repository OpenSpec workflow and skills](AGENTS.md#task-workflow-and-local-skills)
- [Primary references](docs/REFERENCES.md)

## First training target

Four independent CPU processes consume different minibatches, compute gradients with PyTorch, and synchronize them through our native C++ centralized all-reduce. Their losses, averaged gradients, and updated parameters must match a single-process reference using the same combined batches within specified numerical tolerances.

The engine owns socket communication and reduction. PyTorch owns the model, autograd, and initial optimizer. Gloo, MPI, and NCCL are reference implementations or explicit adapters; benchmark baselines remain separate from our collective implementations.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Trainer[PyTorch trainer] --> Bindings[Python bindings]
    Backend[Future torch.distributed adapter] --> Engine[C++ collective engine]
    Bindings --> Engine
    Engine --> TCP[Our TCP transport]
    Engine --> External[Future transport adapters]
    K8s[Kubernetes deployment and job admission] -. launches .-> Trainer
```

The standalone C++ library does not require PyTorch, Python, Kubernetes, or CUDA to build. CUDA and framework integrations are optional layers.

## Development and validation direction

Linux is the primary runtime. Development can use Ubuntu under WSL2; Linux containers provide a reproducible deployment environment. Native Windows support has its own milestone.

The currently available machine has one NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU with approximately 12 GB VRAM. This permits CUDA integration tests. Shared-GPU tests and local containers do not establish multi-GPU or physical multi-host scaling; those results have a separate hardware-dependent milestone.

Later work covers ring and tree collectives, GPU transfers and overlap, reduce-scatter/all-gather, sharded Adam states, checkpoint recovery, Kubernetes deployment with exclusive job-token pools, external transports, and a PyTorch communication backend.

milestones.title: M1 — Correct CPU engine and trainer
milestones.description: Own the complete CPU communication path: standalone C++ TCP engine, centralized FP32 SUM all-reduce, Python bindings, and a deterministic four-process trainer. Completion: Losses, averaged gradients, and updated parameters match the same combined-batch reference; real process/container tests and bounded failure behavior pass. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M2 — CUDA training functionality
milestones.description: Make GPU training use our engine through an explicit host-staged CUDA adapter while preserving the optional CPU-only build. Completion: One-GPU functional training parity, correct stream/buffer lifetime, and separate measurements of copies, reduction, and communication. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M3 — Collective algorithms and CPU benchmarks
milestones.description: Implement ring and tree collectives and explain their measured behavior against a comparable CPU baseline. Completion: Correct odd-rank/uneven-size cases, reproducible Gloo comparisons, raw samples, and a calibrated ring-model analysis. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M4 — CUDA reductions and backward overlap
milestones.description: Develop asynchronous progress, native CUDA reductions, pipelined staging, and ordered gradient-bucket overlap. Completion: Correct delayed-rank/error behavior, native CUDA reduction tests, and measured timelines on a tiny transformer; no unsupported multi-GPU claims. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M5 — Sharding collectives and ZeRO-1 Adam
milestones.description: Expose reduce-scatter/all-gather and implement simplified Adam optimizer-state sharding with replicated parameters and gradients. Completion: Collective conformance, ordinary-Adam parameter/state parity, and separate optimizer-state memory accounting. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M6 — Consistent checkpoints and group recovery
milestones.description: Recover an interrupted training job by restarting its fixed-size worker group from the latest committed consistent checkpoint. Completion: Atomic checkpoint publication, bounded retry/cleanup, and kill/restart parity; sharded-state coverage follows M5. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M7 — Kubernetes and exclusive token admission
milestones.description: Integrate existing Kubernetes orchestration with whole-group resource readiness and exclusive weighted job-token pools. Completion: Deployment/recovery tests plus atomic per-job admission, non-borrowing/non-preemptive policy, FIFO ordering, and restart-safe accounting. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M8 — Framework and transport adapters
milestones.description: Attach existing libraries through an MPI point-to-point transport and a versioned custom PyTorch communication backend. Completion: Optional dependencies, common conformance tests, training parity, and explicit supported-version/device coverage. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M9 — Native Windows portability
milestones.description: Build and run the engine natively on Windows through the isolated networking boundary. Completion: Winsock implementation, native package/build, local multi-process CPU collectives, and reference training parity. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

milestones.title: M10 — Physical multi-host and multi-GPU validation
milestones.description: Validate real host/device topology and fair GPU scaling once external hardware is available. Completion: Distinct-GPU NCCL comparisons, physical multi-host execution, raw results and environment/topology records. Requires additional hardware. No due date; see docs/ROADMAP.md.

projects.name: FlowForge
projects.summary: Event-driven automation in .NET. From trigger conditions to jobs running across distributed worker hosts.
projects.readme:
# FlowForge

A workflow orchestration system built in .NET 10. Users define **Automations** — trigger conditions that automatically create and dispatch **Jobs** to distributed worker hosts for execution.

## Architecture

```
┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌───────────────────┐
│   Frontend  │────▶│   Web API    │────▶│  Redis Streams    │
└─────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────┬────────────┘
                                                 │
              ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬────┘
              ▼              ▼              ▼
       ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐
       │  Job       │ │  Job       │ │  Workflow  │
       │ Automator  │ │Orchestrator│ │   Host     │
       └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └─────┬──────┘
                                           │ spawns
                                      ┌────▼──────┐
                                      │ Workflow  │
                                      │  Engine   │
                                      └───────────┘
```

| Service | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Web API** | REST endpoints, SignalR real-time updates, webhook ingestion |
| **Job Automator** | Evaluates trigger conditions, publishes job creation events |
| **Job Orchestrator** | Consumes job events, assigns jobs to hosts via round-robin |
| **Workflow Host** | Receives assigned jobs, manages engine child processes |
| **Workflow Engine** | Executes a single job, reports progress via Redis |

## Prerequisites

- [.NET 10 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download)
- [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop)
- Python 3 (only needed locally for `custom-script` triggers outside Docker)

## Quick Start

**1. Start infrastructure**

```bash
cd deploy/docker
docker compose up -d
```

This starts:
- `flowforge-db-platform` — PostgreSQL (port 5432) — automations, host groups
- `flowforge-db-minion` — PostgreSQL (port 5433) — jobs for the `Minion` host group
- `flowforge-db-titan` — PostgreSQL (port 5434) — jobs for the `Titan` host group
- `flowforge-db-quartz` — PostgreSQL (port 5435) — Quartz.NET clustered job store
- `flowforge-redis` — Redis (port 6379) — event streams and trigger flags
- `flowforge-jaeger` — Jaeger (UI: port 16686, OTLP: port 4317) — distributed traces

**2. Run the services**

```bash
dotnet run --project src/services/FlowForge.WebApi
dotnet run --project src/services/FlowForge.JobAutomator
dotnet run --project src/services/FlowForge.JobOrchestrator
dotnet run --project src/services/FlowForge.WorkflowHost
```

The Web API starts on `http://localhost:5015`. Migrations are applied automatically on startup.

**3. Run tests**

```bash
dotnet test
```

## Key Concepts

### Automation

Combines one or more **Triggers** with a **Condition** (AND/OR tree) and targets a **Host Group**. When enabled and all conditions are met, a **Job** is created.

### Trigger Types

| Type ID | Description |
|---|---|
| `schedule` | Fires on a cron schedule (6-part, UTC) |
| `sql` | Fires when a SQL query returns a non-empty result set |
| `job-completed` | Fires when a specific job finishes |
| `webhook` | Fires on HTTP POST to `/api/automations/{id}/webhook` |
| `custom-script` | Fires when a user-provided Python 3 script exits 0 and prints `true` |

### Job Status Lifecycle

```
Pending → Started → InProgress → Completed
                              └→ Error
                              └→ CompletedUnsuccessfully
       └→ Removed
       → Cancel → Cancelled
```

### Host Groups

A named pool of Workflow Host instances, each with its own dedicated jobs database (`ConnectionId`).

## Observability

Distributed traces are exported via OTLP to Jaeger. Open `http://localhost:16686` to explore traces across all services.

Each service emits spans under `FlowForge.{ServiceName}`. Trace context is propagated through Redis Stream messages via the `traceparent` field.

## Project Structure

```
src/
  shared/
    FlowForge.Domain          # Entities, value objects, domain exceptions
    FlowForge.Contracts       # Event DTOs shared across services
    FlowForge.Infrastructure  # EF Core, Redis messaging, Quartz, telemetry
  services/
    FlowForge.WebApi
    FlowForge.JobAutomator
    FlowForge.JobOrchestrator
    FlowForge.WorkflowHost
    FlowForge.WorkflowEngine
deploy/
  docker/
    compose.yaml
    quartz-postgresql.sql     # Quartz.NET DDL, auto-applied on first container start
docs/
  AGENTS.md        # Full system overview for AI agents
  CONVENTIONS.md   # Coding standards and DDD rules
  SPECS.md         # Solution structure and database schema
  TRIGGERS.md      # Trigger type system and config schemas
  WEBAPI.md        # REST endpoints and background workers
  JOBAUTOMATOR.md  # Trigger evaluation and Quartz scheduling
  JOBORCHESTRATOR.md
  WORKFLOWHOST.md
  WORKFLOWENGINE.md
```
